analysis.one_liner: Lets doctors who own hospitals refer their Medicare patients to their own facilities again.
analysis.headline: Eleven Senate Republicans backed the repeal, but the Finance Committee never took it up and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would wipe out the Affordable Care Act rules that stopped doctors from building new physician-owned hospitals and then sending their own Medicare patients to them for profit. Those rules were written to curb a conflict of interest: a doctor who profits from every scan, surgery, or bed-night ordered has a built-in reason to order more. Repealing them would reopen that channel, letting physician investors expand their hospitals and bill Medicare for the care they themselves decide patients need.
analysis.who_benefits: Physicians who own or invest in hospitals. They could once again construct new hospitals or add beds, physician offices, and imaging machines, then refer their own patients there and earn a return on every service delivered. Medicare would pay for that care, so revenue would come from federal funds and beneficiary copays rather than from patients shopping on price.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the ACA sections (6001 and 10601) and the reconciliation-act section (1106) that restricted the Medicare exception to the ban on physicians referring patients to hospitals in which they hold an ownership stake, restoring the rules as if those sections had never been enacted.
Supporters argue physician-owned hospitals offer high-quality care and that lifting the construction limits would increase competition and access in some markets.
Medicare payment would cover the services performed at newly built or expanded physician-owned hospitals, giving the facilities a federal revenue stream as they grow.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare and its beneficiaries would bear the added cost of self-referred care: a doctor who profits from ordering a service has an incentive to order more, and studies cited when the ACA restrictions were enacted found higher utilization and spending at physician-owned hospitals. Community hospitals would also lose their most profitable cases (heart, orthopedic, imaging) while physician-owned facilities could select profitable patients, leaving community hospitals with more of the uninsured and expensive care.

drawbacks.text: Self-referral creates a conflict of interest: physicians who own the facility profit from the volume of services they personally order, which is the problem the repealed ACA sections were designed to address.
Physician-owned hospitals tend to draw profitable, well-insured patients and lucrative service lines, which can strain community hospitals that must absorb emergency care and unprofitable patients.

An honest supporter would acknowledge that the bill repeals the restrictions wholesale rather than reforming them, restoring the pre-2010 rules rather than crafting a narrower conflict-of-interest standard.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is real but narrow: some patients gain access to physician-owned facilities they like, and competition can work in a few markets. The downside is structural — the bill removes the safeguard against doctors profiting from their own referral decisions, and Medicare pays the bill for any resulting extra volume. On balance the costs fall broadly on taxpayers and sicker patients while the gains go to a specific set of physician investors, which is why Congress restricted self-referral in the first place.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never held a markup or vote, and the bill died there when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Lankford introduced the bill on May 16, 2017, joined by nine other Republican cosponsors, making 11 Republican sponsors in all.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; no further action appears in the record.
The Finance Committee never reported the bill, so the full Senate never voted on it before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The ACA restrictions on physician self-referral stayed in place, which leaves community hospitals and Medicare beneficiaries shielded from the added costs; the physician-investor hospital industry did not get the expansion it sought.

for.name: Sen. James Lankford
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to repeal the ACA limits on physician-owned hospital self-referral.

for.name: 9 Senate Republican cosponsors
for.role: Original cosponsors (Barrasso, Cornyn, Boozman, Cassidy, Cotton, Crapo, Inhofe, Tillis, Young)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it an all-Republican slate of 11 supporters.

for.name: Physician Hospitals of America
for.what_they_did: Lobbied Congress for years to repeal the ACA's physician-owned hospital construction limits.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction for Medicare legislation
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no markup, no vote — leaving the bill to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: American Hospital Association
against.role: Trade association for community and system hospitals
against.what_they_did: Opposed repealing the self-referral limits, arguing they protect community hospitals from losing profitable patients and services.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 sponsors were Republicans in a Senate with 52 Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and no vote was ever taken to test broader support.

industries.note: Repeal would let physician investors build and expand hospitals again and profit from referring their own Medicare patients to them. Their gain comes from billing Medicare for services their ownership stakes incentivize them to order.
Physician-owned facilities can select profitable patients and service lines, leaving community hospitals with emergency and unprofitable care. Public hospital groups opposed repeal for this reason.
Self-referral is associated with higher utilization, so repealing the limits would raise federal and beneficiary costs for care the referring physician profits from.
